scenes.title: 같은 곳을 보는데 기계처럼 느껴지는 이유
lines: Two geese look different ways at the water’s edge. One tips its bill down at the bench while its body lingers behind. The final target may be identical even if the route to it differs. In Clock Tower 3, Alyssa’s body slows while her gaze keeps searching. The path of the head preserves that timing. We'll separate the rotation axes, examine the head and wrist paths, offset their timing, and finish with the eyes. A rotation axis is the line around which something turns. A door rotates around the line through its hinges. In 3D we can describe rotations around three distinct axes. Watch the head nod, turn left or right, and tilt to the side. At the bench, the goose reaches with its bill. The long neck makes the downward and sideways parts easy to see separately. Turning only from side to side can make the head look like an object on a turntable. Small movements on another axis can give the body a more organic action. Two axes are a way of designing the path, not a requirement for every motion.

scenes.title: 숙였다가 돌리기, 기울이면서 돌리기
lines: Keep the starting and ending poses and change the path between them. The first head turns directly to the side. The second looks down a little, then turns. The third tilts slightly on the way to the same target. When Alyssa looks one way and then back, watch the gap between ear and shoulder. Its changing size gives away the tilt. They finish facing the same way, but they get there differently. The numbers make this clear. We'll keep the final yaw at sixty degrees in all three versions. The second adds a ten-degree nod midway and then straightens. Watch Link rise. His chin tips upward while the shoulder lingers nearer the ground. Ten and sixty are settings for this comparison. They let us isolate the effect of changing one element.

scenes.title: 손목과 어깨를 함께 보기
lines: The same difference shows up in a wrist. When Link takes the Sheikah Slate, the wrist does more than turn. Both arms move forward to support the bottom and side. Turning a wrist only around one axis can look like a drill. Tilt it a little first and the hand follows a different path. The wrist also belongs to an arm and a body. Turning a handle can move the hand, shoulder and collarbone as well as rotate the wrist. As the Slate rises, the hands move higher on screen and the Slate tilts. One is a change of position; the other is rotation. Separate a change in orientation from translation through space. On the same handle, rotate the wrist, add tilt, then carry the movement through the shoulder. From one camera, see which addition gives the gesture continuity.

scenes.title: 각 축이 움직이는 시각을 조절하기
lines: Choosing multiple axes is only the beginning. A nod and a turn can start together, or one can lead the other. That slight timing offset changes the flow. Watch the goose lower its neck near the gardener. Follow the bill first, then see when the body follows. An animation curve shows how a value changes over time. Time runs horizontally and the rotation value runs vertically. Separate curves show nod and turn while the playhead matches the pose at that instant. Keep the duration fixed and start one axis a little earlier. Easing adjusts how quickly the change progresses between its beginning and end. Alongside easing, choose which motion leads. On the stairs, watch the face, then the upper body turn toward us. That order gives us a reason to offset the curves. A small move in the opposite direction can add anticipation. The curves let us adjust that flow through the body.

scenes.title: 같은 끝 자세에 다른 성격 담기
lines: Return to the original head turn. Turning up from below, down from above, or with a sideways tilt can suggest different attitudes toward the same target. Alyssa is looking around for a stranger. The surrounding situation changes how we read the same turn. Comparing only the final pose misses that information. No path guarantees a particular emotion. Context, facial expression and speed work together. When two geese share the scene and one turns its head, we can tell which one is interested in the object. The small movement has a job. We're comparing several performances that arrive at the same final pose. Overlay the matching end poses, then play at normal speed to see the difference the path conveys.

scenes.title: 머리가 아니라 눈까지 목표를 보게 하기
lines: Finally, check the eyes. With a temporary face whose eyes don't move, it's easy to aim the whole head at the target. Adding gaze later can reveal that you turned the head farther than necessary. Look at Link inspecting the Slate. His chin faces nearly forward while his eyes are directed toward the object in his hands. We'll fix the target and switch the eye movement off and on. When the eyes take part of the turn, the head can turn less. Show head direction and eye direction separately to see how they combine. A lively rotation involves more than setting a final angle. Back in the hallway, we first read the intention to find someone. Then we can break down which part moved when. Consider the axis paths and timing, the connected arm and body, and the final gaze together. Design that journey and even a short turn can convey the character's intent.
